headline: Highest risk is medium: shared filesystem and MCP/tool surfaces create prompt-injection, leakage, and write-conflict pathways between Continue and ECC.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue reads workspace files and uses MCP; ECC also uses MCP and writes to shared files under ~/.claude and ~/.cursor/ecc. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if one agent consumes the other's outputs from the shared filesystem or MCP artifacts. No explicit provenance tracking is shown for either agent.
conditions: IF either agent ingests files written by the other as instructions or tool directives, injection becomes active.
IF a shared MCP server or shared workspace is used without provenance tags, attacker-controlled content can steer downstream actions.
mitigations: Separate the two agents into distinct workspaces.
Disable automatic ingestion of shared files as instructions.
Require provenance labels on MCP/file inputs.
Review and whitelist MCP servers before enabling them.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents read and write filesystem content, and Continue touches source code/open editor buffers while ECC touches session summaries, skills, hooks, and security findings. Because shared state is explicitly via filesystem, sensitive material can flow from one agent's workspace into the other's outputs in default use unless isolated.
conditions: IF both agents point at the same home directory or workspace, file contents can cross between them.
IF either agent uploads file contents to its backend during normal operation, shared sensitive data can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Use separate OS users or home directories.
Move one agent to a dedicated workspace.
Audit which files each agent reads before enabling it.
Restrict secrets in shared folders.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell, subprocess, and MCP access; ECC also modifies git state. The profiles show shared state via filesystem, so concurrent edits can collide on files, hooks, and repo state. Because one agent can change git while the other writes workspace files, the conflict can corrupt work or overwrite changes by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or config tree, concurrent writes can race.
IF ECC modifies git state while Continue writes workspace files, repository state can become inconsistent.
mitigations: Run only one agent per repo at a time.
Use file locks around shared paths.
Disable git-mutating actions in ECC for shared repos.
Snapshot the workspace before multi-agent runs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue produces coding assistance from workspace context, and ECC exposes skills, hooks, and session summaries that can be treated as authoritative workflow inputs. If ECC consumes Continue's generated code or findings without verification, errors can cascade into further edits or automation. The pair lacks any documented verification boundary in the profiles.
conditions: IF ECC uses Continue-generated code, findings, or summaries as authoritative input, downstream mistakes can propagate.
IF either agent auto-applies the other's suggestions without human review, error amplification occurs.
mitigations: Require human review before applying suggestions.
Mark generated artifacts as untrusted by default.
Separate drafting from execution roles.
Add a verification checklist for cross-agent handoffs.
requires-engineering: implement confidence/provenance gating.

E_compliance.rationale: ECC handles session summaries, metrics, hooks, and security findings, while Continue handles source code and open editor buffers. The profiles do not show a residency or regulated-data mismatch, so only a limited compliance gap is visible from docs. Continue is open-source and ECC is source-available, but that alone does not establish a breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into ECC session summaries or hooks and then synced to external services, compliance risk increases.
IF the deployment requires a specific residency or retention policy not shown in the profiles, the gap becomes material.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared prompts.
Review retention settings before use.
Disable unnecessary sync or external integrations.
Document data classes allowed in each agent.
requires-engineering: map residency and retention controls explicitly.
